newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Belarus nuclear missiles could be useful to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Belarus nuclear missiles could be useful to Russia.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

A handful of former Soviet nuclear missiles in troubled Belarus pose no military threat but might be used as a political weapon by Russia in its fight against NATO expansion, Western diplomats and analysts say.

Moscow controls all of the former Soviet nuclear arsenal, the world's largest, and almost all weapons -- short and long-range -- have been withdrawn to Russia from their original bases in Kazakhstan, Ukraine and Belarus.
Only 18 SS-25 intercontinental missiles remain outside Russia, in Belarus, although controlled by Russian forces.
With President Alexander Lukashenko locked in a bitter power struggle with parliament, international concern is growing over the wider security implications of the crisis.

Western military officials and experts say the weapons could not be used by Belarus, even in the unlikely event that it seized them from Russian control. But there are concerns that Moscow and Minsk might exploit them for diplomatic aims.

"The threat from these weapons is not military, it's political," said one Western envoy. "Belarus and Russia both oppose NATO expansion and either of them might decide to use the missile issue to make a point."
"There is no way of launching these weapons unless Russia decided to use them," said Stephen Young of the British American Security Information Council (BASIC) in London.

Lukashenko has already hinted he could keep the weapons, single-warhead missiles which can reach the United States, in protest at NATO's plans to take in former communist states -- despite a promise to ship them back to Russia by year-end.

Belarus shares a border with Poland, expected to be among the first nations to join the 16-nation alliance, and could ask Russia to leave the weapons in Belarus to fend off what it sees as a threat from the West.

Moscow would risk a major row with the United States if it reneged on promises to take back all nuclear weapons and some diplomats and analysts do not think Russia would risk losing international credibility, not to mention aid, as a result.
"The Russians are very careful about this sort of thing and besides, they want the missiles back," said Rose Gottemoeller of the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London.

While most multiple-warhead missiles are to be destroyed under U.S.-Russian arms treaties, single warhead missiles like the SS-25 can be retained. Based on mobile launchers, the SS-25 is the best weapon in Russia's nuclear arsenal and expensive.

But others say Russia might agree to delays in returning the weapons, as one of the few concrete actions it could take against the West over NATO expansion, or to try and win concessions from the alliance over enlargement.

"For now the Russian official line is very responsible but it is something they could consider in the future," said Roy Allison, an expert on Russian security at the Royal Institute of International Affairs (RIIA) in London.
At a conference in Stockholm on Tuesday, Russia's ambassador to Sweden said enlarging NATO without Moscow's consent would mean renewed reliance on nuclear weapons.
"This is a real danger for the United States and Europe," Ambassador Oleg Grinevsky told the security conference.

Russia's military is keen to develop cooperation with Belarus and use it as a bastion to protect the Western and Baltic approaches, protection that collapsed when the Warsaw Pact and Soviet Union fell apart.
Lukashenko, diplomats say, may play on this Russian need to enhance its own security to try and hang on to the missiles -- but would not try to seize them from Moscow's control.
"Russia is his only strategic partner and he knows that Moscow would not allow that to happen," said Allison.
Concern has also grown in the West over Russian nuclear security, although one intelligence source told Reuters the missiles in Belarus appeared to be well-protected.
As weapons, the missiles would be useless to Minsk.
Codes to permit launch and pick targets come from Moscow and there are complex devices to prevent unauthorised use.
"You can't just walk in to the base, push aside the guy who has his finger on the button and then threaten a launch," said one Western security source familiar with nuclear issues.
"It doesn't work like that. Thank God."
